    Angelly v. US (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca13-25-01333 / USCOURTS-ca13-25-01333-0

    FAPD-AI: Landowners in Illinois and Kentucky challenged the Army Corps of Engineers' river management practices, alleging that dam construction and dike placement caused increased flooding on their properties constituting a taking of property under the Fifth Amendment. The trial court dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction, finding the evidence did not establish that a new flooding pattern had emerged within the applicable statute of limitations period. The Federal Circuit affirmed, concluding the trial court's analysis of hydrographical data contained no clear error. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 18:28:25 Eastern time ET
    Crider v. Collins (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca13-25-01494 / USCOURTS-ca13-25-01494-0

    FAPD-AI: Raymond Crider, a veteran with a service-connected PTSD rating, appealed the Board of Veterans' Appeals' denial of his claim for total disability rating based on individual unemployability for the period prior to his PTSD rating's increase to 100% in March 2021. The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal, finding it lacked jurisdiction to review the application of a regulation to specific facts, as Crider's arguments concerned the Board's factual determinations regarding his employment capacity rather than the interpretation of the regulation itself. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Edwards V. Brown, Et AL. (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca9-25-6849 / USCOURTS-ca9-25-6849-0

    FAPD-AI: Deymon Edwards sued Oregon correctional officers under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for denying him a decontamination shower after he was exposed to pepper spray in October 2022. The district court dismissed his claims as time-barred under Oregon's two-year statute of limitations, but the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that Oregon tolling law required the statute to be tolled during Edwards's required prison grievance process. Edwards's January 2025 filing was timely because tolling ran from when he initiated his grievance in October 2022 until he exhausted his administrative remedies in January 2023. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:13:35 Eastern time ET
    United States of America, Et AL. V. Burton, Et AL. (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca9-25-87 / USCOURTS-ca9-25-87-0

    FAPD-AI: Air Force employees sued Jeremy Burton, a former Deputy Chief Information Officer, under the False Claims Act for allegedly coordinating with a defense contractor to direct government contracts in violation of federal acquisition regulations. Burton invoked a statutory bar to suits against members of the armed forces, but the district court concluded he was a civilian employee and therefore not protected by the bar. The Ninth Circuit dismissed Burton's interlocutory appeal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that the statutory bar is a jurisdictional bar rather than an immunity subject to immediate appellate review. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:13:35 Eastern time ET
    Wanyu Zhang v. National Public Radio, Inc. (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-caDC-25-07207 / USCOURTS-caDC-25-07207-0

    FAPD-AI: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit affirmed a district court order dismissing Wanyu Zhang's Title VII national origin discrimination complaint against National Public Radio. The court found that Zhang failed to allege sufficient facts showing that NPR took adverse action against her based on national origin, and that NPR's stated reasons for termination—lack of work authorization and concerns about visa application responses—were not challenged as inaccurate or pretextual. The court also found that Zhang forfeited an administrative remedies exhaustion challenge by raising it only briefly in her appeal. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:13:34 Eastern time ET
    Diemert V. City of Seattle (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca9-25-1188 / USCOURTS-ca9-25-1188-0

    FAPD-AI: Joshua Diemert, a white employee of Seattle's Human Services Department, alleged that the City's Race and Social Justice Initiative created a racially hostile work environment and violated Title VII and state civil rights law. The Ninth Circuit reversed the summary judgment dismissal of his hostile work environment claims, finding material facts in dispute regarding whether workplace incidents were sufficiently severe and pervasive to alter his employment conditions. The court affirmed dismissal of his constructive discharge, disparate treatment, retaliation, and Equal Protection claims. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:13:34 Eastern time ET
    State of Washington, Et AL. V. Crown Resources Corporation, Et AL. (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca9-25-2397 / USCOURTS-ca9-25-2397-0

    FAPD-AI: The State of Washington and a private environmental organization filed separate citizen suits under the Clean Water Act against Crown Resources Corporation for alleged violations at the Buckhorn Mountain Mine. After the cases were consolidated, the environmental organization settled with Crown without involving Washington, and the district court dismissed Washington's claims as barred by claim preclusion. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that Washington was not bound by the consent decree because it was not a party to it or in privity with the settling organization. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:13:32 Eastern time ET
    Brooke Mason v. Cook County, Illinois (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-25-02743 / USCOURTS-ca7-25-02743-0

    FAPD-AI: Brooke Mason appealed her termination from a Cook County hospital pharmacy position after she refused the COVID-19 vaccine on religious grounds, claiming Title VII religious discrimination. The Seventh Circuit affirmed that Cook County could deny religious accommodation without suffering undue hardship, given Mason's role involving close patient contact and employee interaction during a public health crisis. The court found that masking and social distancing alone did not adequately reduce risks to patient and employee safety. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:13:32 Eastern time ET
    FTC v. Andrew Lloyd (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-25-03049 / USCOURTS-ca7-25-03049-0

    FAPD-AI: Andrew Lloyd settled a 2017 False Claims Act enforcement action brought by the FTC, paying $645,000 and waiving his right to challenge the judgment. In 2025, Lloyd moved to vacate the judgment, citing autism, nondisclosure of a criminal referral, and a 2021 Supreme Court precedent. The Seventh Circuit affirmed dismissal, finding Lloyd barred by his settlement waiver, his motion untimely, and the Supreme Court precedent inapplicable. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Fifth Circuit denied Mirian Anabel Robles-Zuniga's petition for review of the Board of Immigration Appeals' dismissal of her asylum, withholding of removal, and Convention Against Torture claims.     FAPD-AI: The Sixth Circuit affirmed Eduardo Rafael Lopez-Escarrega's conviction for being found in the United States illegally after previous removal under 8 U.S.C. § 1326(a), rejecting his duress defense based on alleged cartel threats and his Speedy Trial Act and sentencing challenges.     FAPD-AI: The States Handling Access to Reciprocity for Employment Act of 2026 authorizes the FBI to provide criminal history record information to state licensing authorities for occupational and professional licensing purposes under interstate compacts.     Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr2481enr

    FAPD-AI: The Romance Scam Prevention Act requires online dating service providers to notify members within 24 hours (or up to three days in certain circumstances) when they have received messages from members whose accounts have been banned for fraud risk, including the username of the banned member, warnings about false identities, and information about fraud prevention best practices. The Federal Trade Commission enforces the law, and providers are granted liability protection for complying with these notification requirements. BILLS-SEL-01
